# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([merge-to-main/SKILL.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.

Pack adoption interview pending — the active packs below declare adoption questions this project has not answered. In an INTERACTIVE session, at a natural moment (not mid-task), ask the owner each question via AskUserQuestion, record the answer VERBATIM in .claudinite-checks.json on that pack's entry as answers: { "<question-id>": "<answer>" } ("n/a — none wanted" is a valid answer and stops the asking), and where the question carries a distill note, derive the entry's config from the answer. This is a mild reminder, never a gate: in an unattended session, or when it would derail the work at hand, ignore it entirely and leave it for a later interactive session.
- claude-code-web-users-support / store: Where do this project's people keep their personal interaction preferences — the repository holding one `<email>.md` per person? Give an `owner/name` (a fleet usually has one repo for this), or say "n/a — none" if this project has no such store. [distill: the answer's `owner/name` becomes this entry's `config.repo` (add `config.path` only when the files do not sit in `preferences/`); "n/a" leaves the entry without a config and the preferences feature inert]
- executable-requirements / ui_testing: How are the executable UI requirements exercised — what is the UI-testing mechanism (browser/E2E such as Playwright, DOM-level golden rendering, a headless harness), or is there none yet? Most requirements should be verifiable by a short test that drives to a state and makes a VISUAL assertion (a committed golden the owner checks by sight), so this fixes how a requirement becomes that assertion. [distill: recorded as intent; it fixes the harness the requirements.md drives its UI gates through, and the visual-golden path most leaves take for simplest owner verification]

Name the path or source so the spec is seeded from it rather than reinvented. [distill: record the source; set config.spec to the executable spec's home (default dev/requirements/requirements.md) and extract the initial requirements from the named source]
- product-wiki / product: What is the product — what does it do, and what is the core value it delivers? If the repo already carries a product brief or spec, read it and confirm rather than asking cold. ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:

PR you open `product-wiki-growth` so the next round's precondition can see it.

## Method

1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, 140 characters each — about one line) — so a new insight
   that belongs at the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Each bullet is one
   finding in plain words: no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, and preferably something a reader
   who knows the field would *not* already assume. Judging obviousness is hard, so when in doubt keep the
   line rather than agonising — short and slightly obvious beats long and careful. Rewrite a bullet the run
   superseded (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone
   when the run changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a
   table of contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
   surfaced.

Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.

A unique branch per run, commits touching only `product-wiki/**` minus `product-requirements/`, one
**PR — never merged, never pushed to the default branch directly** — carrying the **`product-wiki-growth`
label**. The label is load-bearing: it is how the next run's preflight sees this PR at all, so a PR opened
without it will be stacked on by the following slot.
Web-researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. PR body: the question(s)
researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.

1	# Competitors
2	
3	A self-growing survey of tools competing to do what this extension does: get an
4	event from a webpage onto a calendar with minimal friction. Not exhaustive — a
5	general lay of the land, kept current by the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's
6	growth worker (mounted read-only under `.claudinite/`).
7	Sibling to [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md) (the calendar-market
8	landscape) and [`../Users/`](../Users/README.md) (who uses this
9	extension).
10	
11	## Landscape (as of 2026-07-15)
12	
13	| Tool | Approach | Notes |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| [Eventy](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/eventy/kfancgcbhdkeohknmidbnioccmmoknjl) | AI extraction from webpages, email, flyers, concert posters, even screenshots | Broadest input surface of the group; 4.4★ on the Chrome Web Store. Exports to Google Calendar or `.ics` (Outlook/Apple Calendar) — covers the multi-calendar gap this project doesn't (see Market open question). |
16	| [Add To Calendar](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/add-to-calendar/jnbpajadakhkpcncmbfhkgaaoioofkfd) | Highlight text → right-click → "Intelligent Technology" scan for title/date/time/address | 4.4★. Closest in spirit to a lightweight, single-purpose tool rather than a broad AI product. |
17	| [Calendar Event Creator](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/calendar-event-creator/nbdaijdcnmhjhoekcdcgdjcjheajgpad) | Select event text → right-click → OpenAI API extracts details | Requires an OpenAI-backed flow — a real friction point vs. "no API key" positioning. |
18	| [ChatGPT for Google Calendar](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/chatgpt-for-google-calend/laejdmahdkleahgkdpiapfdcmleedhca) | LLM-based extraction of title/date/time/location from any webpage | Google-Calendar-only, like this project, but LLM-dependent rather than rule-based + generic-fallback. |
19	| [Smart Calendars AI](https://www.smartcalendars.ai/en/articles/browser-extension-add-events) | "Turns what you're reading into ready-to-review calendar events" | Cross-browser (Chrome + Safari) — worth tracking if Safari support ever becomes relevant here. |
20	| [CalendarAdd](https://github.com/mattkrins/CalendarAdd) | Open-source Chrome extension: select text → Google Calendar event | Same "no server, no account" spirit as this project, but text-selection-only (no per-site structured extraction, no JSON-LD awareness). |
21	| Axiom.ai / Bardeen | General no-code browser-automation platforms; calendar event creation is one of many workflows, not a dedicated product | Not direct competitors for a casual user, but relevant if "add to calendar" ever gets framed as one automation among many rather than a single-purpose tool. |
22	
23	## Positioning takeaways
24	
25	- **Most competitors lean on a cloud AI/LLM API** (OpenAI or similar) for
26	  extraction, which typically means an account, a subscription, or at least a
27	  network call to a third party with the page's content. This project's
28	  rule-based per-site extractors + generic fallback (no OAuth, no API key, no
29	  content leaves the browser) is a real, defensible differentiator — worth
30	  stating explicitly in messaging/store listing copy, not just an implementation

1	# Domain
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the **problem domain** this extension models: how events
4	are represented on the web, and how those representations shape what the
5	extension can extract. Where [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md),
6	[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md), and
7	[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) cover the outside actors (the
8	platforms, the people, the rivals), this wiki covers the *thing itself* — the
9	event data, formats, and page shapes the extractor has to make sense of. It is
10	the knowledge that most directly drives extraction requirements.
11	
12	## Machine-readable event formats (as of 2026-07-16)
13	
14	Ordered roughly by how useful they are to a rule-based extractor — highest-signal
15	first. The project's stance (see the **architecture rules of the road** section of
16	`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`, where it reads "prefer extracting
17	JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions" — the
18	`dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` this page previously cited was superseded
19	when that doc was folded into the gcec pack) is to **prefer machine-readable
20	markup over brittle DOM scraping**, because it survives redesigns and
21	single-page-app rendering.
22	
23	- **schema.org `Event` as JSON-LD** — the highest-value target and the one Google
24	  actively rewards. Emitted as a standalone `<script type="application/ld+json">`
25	  block, so it is cleanly separable from the page markup and survives client-side
26	  rendering. Google's required properties are **`name`, `startDate`, and
27	  `location`**; `startDate`/`endDate` are ISO-8601 **with a UTC/GMT offset**
28	  (the offset is what lets us derive `ctz` safely — see
29	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js`).
30	  `location` is a `Place` (with `address`: `streetAddress`, `addressLocality`,
31	  `addressRegion`, `postalCode`) or a `VirtualLocation` (URL only) for online
32	  events. Since 2020 Google also expects **`eventAttendanceMode`**
33	  (`Offline`/`Online`/`Mixed`), and as of a June 2025 change requires a **physical
34	  location** for the rich result at all. Recommended extras that often carry real
35	  data: `endDate`, `eventStatus`, `image`, `description`, `offers`.
36	- **Microdata / RDFa** (schema.org vocabulary inline in the HTML) — same
37	  vocabulary, embedded in the markup rather than a separate block. Common on
38	  server-rendered sites; JSON-LD is now preferred and gets new features first, so
39	  microdata/RDFa are a declining but still-present fallback worth reading when no
40	  JSON-LD block exists. Web-wide, Microdata is still material — the *Web Almanac
41	  2024* has it steady on roughly a quarter of pages (~26%), well ahead of
42	  microformats below.
43	- **`h-event` / hCalendar microformats** — an older, class-attribute convention
44	  (`h-event`, `p-name`, `dt-start`, `p-location`). Google added hCalendar event
45	  support back in 2010; adoption has been overtaken by schema.org, but legacy and
46	  indie-web event pages still use it. **A 2026 prevalence check settles whether
47	  they're worth a dedicated reader — no:** the HTTP Archive *Web Almanac 2024*
48	  puts *all* microformats combined below ~1% of pages (hCalendar only a fraction
49	  of that), against JSON-LD at ~41% (up from 34% in 2022) and Microdata steady at
50	  ~26%. So `h-event`/hCalendar is a negligible tail; where it does appear, the
51	  generic text/`og:` fallback is enough. Note: microformats are **not** part of
52	  the schema.org vocabulary, so any dedicated reader would need its own parser —
53	  another reason not to build one for a sub-1% format. **Tooling corroboration
54	  (2026-07-26):** the one browser tool that ever shipped a microformat→calendar
55	  reader at scale — the Google-encouraged "Google Calendar" Chrome extension,
56	  which detected `hCalendar` and derivative microformats on the page and offered
57	  a one-click add — is formally shut down and no longer installable, and the
58	  generic "Microformats" extension that exported `hCalendar` to iCalendar is
59	  likewise reported delisted (unmaintained since ~2014). So there is also no
60	  live microformat event reader left to borrow from (the demand-side reading of
61	  the same fact is in [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)).
62	- **OpenGraph / meta tags** (`og:title`, `og:description`, and event-ish `<meta>`)
63	  — not event-specific, but SPA pages very often still inject them, so they are a
64	  reliable low-fidelity fallback for title/description when nothing structured
65	  exists.
66	- **iCalendar (`.ics` / RFC 5545)** — the interchange format calendars import,
67	  not usually embedded in a page, but the semantic reference for event modelling.
68	  A `VEVENT` carries `DTSTART`/`DTEND` with a **`TZID`** (or a trailing `Z` for
69	  UTC, or a bare **floating** time that means "the same wall-clock time in every
70	  zone"). Recurrence is an **`RRULE`** (`FREQ` = DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/YEARLY plus
71	  `INTERVAL`/`COUNT`/`UNTIL`/`BYDAY`…) expanded from `DTSTART`, with `RDATE`/`EXDATE`
72	  adjustments. This is the vocabulary to match when we reason about timezones and
73	  repeats even though we target Google Calendar's `render` URL, not `.ics`.
74	
75	## Page-shape taxonomy
76	
77	The extractor must first recognise *what kind of event page* it's on — this is the
78	structural decision behind "one button per event":
79	
80	- **Single-event page** — one clear event (a concert, a talk, a venue listing).
81	  Usually one `Event` JSON-LD block or one hero heading + date/venue. The common
82	  case.
83	- **Listing / index page** — a calendar-of-events or search-results page with many
84	  entries, often an array of `Event` objects or repeated cards. Drives the
85	  multiple-buttons behaviour; the generic fallback can't reliably enumerate these
86	  (it recovers the primary event only — see the fallback-coverage gate).
87	- **Series / recurring page** — one event described as repeating (an `RRULE` in
88	  `.ics`, or schema.org `eventSchedule`). A single page can imply many instances;
89	  how many to surface is genuinely undecided (see Open questions).
90	
91	## Timezone & recurrence semantics
92	
93	- **Timezone** is the trust-critical field: a wrong `ctz` is worse than none —
94	  the unanimity rule, stated in the contract header of
95	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` itself (not in the gcec
96	  pack's RULES.md): a zone is returned **only when two independent page-declared
97	  hints agree**, and `""` whenever anything disagrees. The four hint kinds that
98	  file recognises are *stated* (an IANA zone in inline-script JSON), *offset* (the
99	  event's own UTC offset — a trailing `Z` explicitly does **not** count, since
100	  pages habitually serialize in UTC regardless of venue), *country*, and *locale*.
101	  The domain gives three shapes — an
102	  **offset-bearing** instant (ISO-8601 `…+02:00`, or `.ics` `Z`/`TZID`), a
103	  **floating** time (no zone; "same wall-clock everywhere"), and **no time signal
104	  at all**. Only the first lets `ctz` be *derived* rather than guessed.
105	- **Recurrence** (`RRULE`, `eventSchedule`) is currently out of the extension's
106	  scope — it surfaces the event, not its repeat rule. Whether a recurring page
107	  should yield one instance, the next instance, or a note is an open product
108	  question, not a settled requirement. Two 2026 findings narrow *where* the cost
109	  of ever changing that sits:
110	  - **The sink is not the blocker.** Google Calendar's
111	    `render?action=TEMPLATE` link — the exact URL this extension emits — takes an
112	    optional **`recur`** parameter whose value is an RFC-5545 recurrence rule
113	    verbatim: `recur=RRULE:FREQ=DAILY` (`required: no`, `format: text
114	    (RFC-5545 specs)`), and in practice fuller rules such as
115	    `recur=RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;INTERVAL=1;BYDAY=2MO;UNTIL=20250609T000000Z`. So
116	    "hand the user a repeating event" is already expressible in the target we
117	    emit; nothing about the render URL forces the one-instance behaviour.
118	  - **The source side speaks a different vocabulary.** schema.org does *not*
119	    express repeats as an `RRULE` string. A repeating event carries
120	    **`eventSchedule`** → a **`Schedule`**, whose minimum is **`repeatFrequency`
121	    as an ISO-8601 *duration*** (`P1W`, `P1M`, `P1D` — not `FREQ=WEEKLY`),
122	    alongside `byDay` / `byMonth` / `byMonthDay` (e.g. `byDay` as an array of
123	    `https://schema.org/Monday`-style URLs), `scheduleTimezone` (an IANA zone),
124	    `startDate`/`endDate`, `startTime`/`endTime`, and `exceptDate` for
125	    exclusions. Emitting `recur=` from page markup therefore needs a genuine
126	    translation step (`repeatFrequency: P1W` + `byDay` → `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=…`,
127	    `exceptDate` → `EXDATE`), not a pass-through. **That mapping — plus whether
128	    target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all — is the real cost, not the URL.**
129	
130	## Implications for extraction requirements
131	
132	- The format ranking above is *why* the extractor is structured as dedicated
133	  per-site sources + a generic JSON-LD/`og`-first fallback: the machine-readable
134	  layers are the durable signal, the DOM is the last resort.
135	- "An event needs real data, not just a supported host" (gcec pack RULES.md,
136	  *Codebase gotchas*) is a direct consequence of the taxonomy: a host match is
137	  not an `Event` object.
138	- The timezone shapes above are the domain justification for the refusal-to-guess
139	  `ctz` contract — a product-requirements-level stance, distilled in
140	  [`../product-requirements/`](../product-requirements/README.md).
141	- **`Event` JSON-LD is real but a minority signal.** The Google/schema.org usage
142	  statistics (June 2026 dataset) put `schema.org/Event` on **fewer than ~1 million
143	  domains** — an order of magnitude behind common types like `author` (10M+);
144	  Web Data Commons corroborates from the Common Crawl corpus. So a large share of
145	  event pages carry *no* `Event` block, which is exactly why the DOM/text and
146	  `og:`/microdata fallback path (and the fallback-coverage routine) carries real
147	  weight rather than being a rare edge case.
148	- **No dedicated microformats reader is warranted.** The 2026 prevalence check
149	  (see the `h-event` bullet) puts *all* microformats combined under ~1% of pages,
150	  so `h-event`/hCalendar stays a fallback-only concern — extraction effort belongs
151	  on the JSON-LD → Microdata → `og:`/text ladder, not a bespoke hCalendar parser.
152

1	# Market
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the market environment this extension operates in: what
4	calendar platforms exist, what kinds of pages people extract events from, and
5	what usage patterns show up in that market. Distinct from
6	[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md) (who uses *this* extension and how) and
7	[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) (who else builds this).
8	
9	## How this wiki grows
10	
11	This follows Andrej Karpathy's ["LLM Wiki" pattern](https://medium.com/@urvvil08/andrej-karpathys-llm-wiki-create-your-own-knowledge-base-8779014accd5):
12	instead of re-deriving market context from scratch on every question, an agent
13	**compiles** findings into this file once and **refines it in place** on later
14	passes — later runs read what's already here before researching, extend or
15	correct it, cite every claim, and only prune a claim when it's superseded (never
16	silently). The mechanic (schedule, what counts as a real update, when to open a
17	PR) is owned by the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's growth worker (mounted
18	read-only under `.claudinite/`).
19	Nothing in this file is guaranteed current — check the growth log's date and
20	treat older entries as a starting point to verify, not ground truth.
21	
22	## Calendar platform landscape (as of 2026-07-15)
23	
24	- The calendar-app market was valued around **$14.6B in 2025**, projected to grow
25	  at roughly **10.8% CAGR through 2034**.
26	- **Google, Microsoft, and Apple** are the dominant players; Google Calendar and
27	  web Outlook together account for the majority of web-based platform usage.
28	  Google Calendar alone is reported in use at **637,000+ companies** in 2026 (62.6%
29	  US-based).
30	- **Web-based platforms held the largest share (38.2% in 2025)** of the calendar
31	  app market, ahead of native mobile/desktop apps — consistent with this
32	  extension's approach (a browser action, not a native app).
33	- Google Calendar's event-creation URL scheme
34	  (`calendar.google.com/calendar/render?action=TEMPLATE`) — what this extension
35	  targets — has no first-party equivalent this project currently uses for Outlook
36	  or Apple Calendar. Google Calendar is ~23% of the calendar-tool market (6sense),
37	  but the portable multi-calendar path is **`.ics` (RFC 5545)**, not per-vendor
38	  deep links: Outlook, Apple Calendar, and any RFC-5545 app both export and import
39	  it, and existing Chrome extensions (ics2gcal, ICS to GCal) already one-click a
40	  `.ics` into Google Calendar. So the export question is really "emit a standards
41	  `.ics`" rather than "add an Outlook deep link" — the same lever the AI
42	  competitors already pull (Eventy, Smart Calendars AI; see Competitors). Tradeoff:
43	  a `.ics` is a *download*, where the render URL is a no-download click-through —
44	  the exact friction this product optimises away.
45	
46	## Event-source landscape (what pages people extract *from*)
47	
48	Sites the extension already has dedicated extractors for (see
49	`extension/event-extractors/custom/` and `dev/requirements/extractor/`) are
50	themselves representative of the market: ticketing/listing platforms (e.g.
51	Meetup, Ticketmaster) and single-venue/organizer sites. Two broad source shapes
52	recur across the market:
53	
54	- **Single-event pages** — a venue, a talk, a concert; one clear event, often with
55	  `schema.org`/JSON-LD event markup (the highest-signal, most future-proof
56	  extraction target — see the JSON-LD note in the **architecture rules of the
57	  road** section of `.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`; the
58	  `technicalGotchas.md` this line previously cited was superseded when that doc
59	  was folded into the gcec pack).
60	  Machine-readable markup is increasingly common because search engines reward it
61	  (Google's "Events" rich results), which is a structural tailwind for any
62	  extension that prefers JSON-LD/`og:` over brittle DOM scraping — but "common" is
63	  a *page-wide* fact, not an event-specific one, and this line overstated it until
64	  2026-07-26: JSON-LD reaches ~41% of pages and Microdata ~26%, while
65	  `schema.org/Event` specifically is on fewer than ~1M domains. The tailwind is
66	  real; it does not mean most event pages are structured. See
67	  [`../Domain/`](../Domain/README.md)'s format ranking.
68	- **Listing/series pages** — a calendar-of-events page with several entries; the
69	  extension already special-cases "one button per event" for this shape (see
70	  `product-requirements/README.md` requirement 4).
71	
72	## Usage patterns / use cases
73	
74	- **One-off personal use** — someone reads about a concert/talk/meetup in a
75	  newsletter, blog post, or social share and wants it on their calendar
76	  immediately, without leaving the page or typing anything.
77	- **Event discovery browsing** — scanning a listing/aggregator page and adding
78	  several events from one visit.
79	- **Professional scheduling from a webpage** — a conference agenda, a webinar
80	  registration page, an internal event site.
81	
82	## Open questions (for the next growth pass)
83	
84	- How much of the "AI-powered extraction" trend (see competitors wiki) is
85	  actually driven by JS-heavy SPA pages that a rule-based extractor + ScraperAPI
86	  render struggles with, vs. genuine accuracy gains from an LLM?
87	- If multi-calendar export is ever added, does the `.ics`-download step erode the
88	  no-download/no-account friction the render URL avoids? (Weigh against the reach
89	  gain — see the Outlook/`.ics` note above, resolved 2026-07-17.)
90	- What share of "event" pages in the wild already carry `schema.org/Event`
91	  JSON-LD vs. requiring DOM/text heuristics? (Would sharpen the fallback-coverage
92	  routine's generic-extraction priorities too — see
93	  `.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/fallback-extractor-improvements/task.md`.)
94	  **Answered web-wide in Domain, 2026-07-17** — `Event` markup is a minority
95	  signal (fewer than ~1M domains), so the DOM/`og:` fallback path carries real
96	  weight; see [`../Domain/README.md`](../Domain/README.md). What stays open here
97	  is the *per-target-host* split, which only the fallback-coverage corpus can give.
98

109

123	- **2026-07-26 (same pass, second half)** — pointed the RULES.md citation at the
124	  right section (**architecture rules of the road**, not *Codebase gotchas*), and
125	  qualified the "machine-readable markup is increasingly common" claim, which was
126	  true page-wide but overstated for *event* pages specifically — cited the ~41% /

1	# Users
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the people who use (or would use) this extension, and how
4	— usage patterns, personas, and pain points. Its sibling wikis cover the other
5	tools chasing the same job ([`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md))
6	and the broader calendar-market context these users sit in
7	([`../Market/`](../Market/README.md)).
8	
9	## How this wiki grows
10	
11	Same mechanic as Market — the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's growth worker
12	(mounted read-only under `.claudinite/`), following the "LLM Wiki" pattern:
13	compile once, refine in place, cite sources,
14	never silently overwrite.
15	
16	## Personas (initial pass — refine as real usage signal appears)
17	
18	- **The one-click saver.** Reads about a single event (a concert, a talk, a
19	  meetup) somewhere on the web and wants it on their calendar before they forget,
20	  with the least possible friction — no typing, no new account, no app switch.
21	  This is the extension's primary target today (see `product-requirements/`
22	  requirement 1).
23	- **The event browser.** Lands on a listing/series page with several events and
24	  wants to cherry-pick a few — served by the "one button per event" requirement.
25	- **The privacy-conscious user.** Actively avoids extensions that want an OAuth
26	  grant, an account, or send page content to a third-party AI API just to copy a
27	  date into a calendar. This persona is who the "no sign-in, no API key" product
28	  requirement is *for* — see the positioning notes in
29	  [`../Competitors/README.md`](../Competitors/README.md). This concern is
30	  well-grounded, not niche: 2026 studies report **86% of the top-100 Chrome
31	  extensions request high-risk permissions at install**, **52% of AI-branded
32	  extensions collect user data** (~1 in 3 collecting PII), and **71% of extensions
33	  publish no privacy policy** — and Chrome grants permissions at install that
34	  persist across every future update. A rule-based, no-OAuth, no-API-key,
35	  nothing-leaves-the-browser design answers exactly this anxiety.
36	
37	## Usage patterns
38	
39	- Single click → review pre-filled Google Calendar event → save. The extension
40	  deliberately stops short of auto-saving, so the user always reviews before
41	  committing (see `dev/requirements/requirements.md`).
42	- Works from whatever page the user is already on — no search, no lookup, no
43	  separate "paste a URL" step, unlike several competitor tools (see
44	  `../Competitors/README.md`).
45	
46	## Pain points to track (hypotheses — verify with real feedback as it arrives)
47	
48	- Extraction misses or gets a field wrong on a page with unusual markup — the
49	  fallback-coverage routine (`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/fallback-extractor-improvements/`) is the
50	  engineering mechanism that narrows this over time; this wiki tracks it from the
51	  *user* side (which misses actually get reported/matter).
52	- Timezone correctness on pages that don't declare one clearly — see the
53	  unanimity rule in the contract header of
54	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` (a zone is emitted only
55	  when two independent page-declared hints agree, otherwise none). The
56	  `technicalGotchas.md` this line cited until 2026-07-26 was superseded when that
57	  doc was folded into the gcec pack; the rule did **not** move into that pack's
58	  RULES.md, it lives in the source file's own header. A wrong `ctz` is a
59	  trust-breaking failure mode worth watching from the user's perspective — and
60	  because the contract refuses to guess, the *user-visible* failure is usually a
61	  **missing** timezone rather than a wrong one, so the complaint shape to expect
62	  in feedback is "it didn't set the timezone", not "it set the wrong time".
63	- No support yet for calendars other than Google Calendar (see Market's open
64	  question on Outlook/ICS) — track whether this actually blocks real users or is
65	  a hypothetical gap.
66	
67	## Open questions
68	
69	- Do real users cite privacy/permissions as a *reason for choosing* a lightweight
70	  extension, or is it a latent preference they don't act on? (The permission-risk
71	  data above is industry-wide, not this extension's own user feedback.)
72	- Which extraction misses actually get reported vs. silently tolerated — i.e.
73	  which sites matter enough to users to warrant a dedicated extractor?
74	- Does the lack of non-Google-Calendar support actually block real users? (Pairs
75	  with Market's `.ics`-export note.)
76	- On timezone, which complaint shape actually shows up — "wrong time" or "no
77	  timezone at all"? The refusal-to-guess contract predicts the latter dominates;
78	  no real feedback yet either way (surfaced 2026-07-26).
79	
80	## Sources
81	
82	Personas and pain points above are hypotheses seeded from the product's existing
83	design decisions (`dev/procedures/highLevelDesign.md`,
84	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`) and general competitor positioning (see
85	`../Competitors/README.md`'s sources) — not yet from direct user research. Flag this
86	clearly until real user feedback (reviews, issues, support requests) backs a
87	claim here. The one externally-sourced claim so far is the industry
88	permission/privacy data backing the privacy-conscious persona:
89	
90	- [Ranking AI-Powered Chrome Extensions by Privacy Risk in 2026 (Incogni)](https://blog.incogni.com/chrome-extensions-privacy-2026/)
91	- [Chrome Permissions Statistics 2026 (AboutChromebooks)](https://www.aboutchromebooks.com/chrome-permissions-statistics/)
92	- [Enterprise Browser Extension Security Report 2026 (LayerX)](https://go.layerxsecurity.com/browser-extension-security-report-2026)
93	
94	## Growth log
95	
96	- **2026-07-15** — initial seed (folder scaffolding + first pass, hypotheses
97	  pending real user-feedback sourcing).
98	- **2026-07-17** — added the required `## Open questions` section; backed the
99	  privacy-conscious persona with 2026 industry data on extension permission/PII
100	  collection and missing privacy policies (Incogni, AboutChromebooks, LayerX) —
101	  the first externally-sourced claim in this wiki.
102	- **2026-07-26** — corrected a superseded repo reference in the timezone pain
103	  point: `dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` no longer exists (folded into the
104	  gcec pack's `RULES.md`, *Codebase gotchas*), and `derive-timezone.js` lives at
105	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/`. No new user-side research this pass —
106	  the personas and pain points here still await real feedback signal.
107	- **2026-07-26 (same pass, second half)** — corrected the replacement citation
108	  written earlier the same day: the unanimity rule did not move into the gcec
109	  pack's RULES.md, it lives in `derive-timezone.js`'s own contract header. Reading
110	  that contract also yielded a user-side implication worth tracking — refusing to
111	  guess makes a *missing* timezone the expected complaint shape rather than a

# Google Calendar Chrome Extension Shutdown

## Shutdown Notice (Verbatim)

"This Chrome extension is **no longer available to install**, though the source code is available here to fork & modify."

## Reasons for Shutdown

The author provides these explanations:

1. **Time constraints**: "the number of requests I have received from various teams at Google to make changes...far outweigh the amount of time I am able to spend on it."

2. **Lack of official adoption**: He attempted to convince Google's Calendar team to adopt the extension as an official product, but they declined.

3. **Project longevity**: Originally conceived as a hackathon project over a decade ago, it was never intended as a long-term personal maintenance commitment.

4. **User scale**: Managing 5 million+ users became unsustainable for a side project.

## Blog Post Link

The provided content contains **no link to an extended shutdown blog post or announcement**—only the GitHub README explanation.

## Technical Details

The README excerpt above does **not mention** detection methods (microformats, page parsing) or user counts beyond the reference to "5 MM+ users" in the shutdown notice.

# Google Calendar CRX Extension: Authorization Requirements

## OAuth Implementation

The extension uses **OAuth protocol** for account authentication. According to the documentation: "Google Calendar for Chrome 1.5+ uses the industry-standard OAuth protocol to fetch your calendar."

## Why Separate Sign-In Was Necessary

Google discontinued an earlier authentication method. The extension required OAuth because: "Google turned off version 2 of the Google Calendar Data API in November 2014, which had earlier made it possible to re-use your browser credentials."

## Features Dependent on Authorization

The documentation does not explicitly detail which specific features (agenda preview, quick add, etc.) depend on OAuth. However, the authorization process is necessary to access calendar data generally, as users must grant permission for the extension to retrieve their calendar information.

## Key Statement on Account Access

Users questioned why separate login was needed despite existing Google Calendar access: "This is no longer permitted, and all apps at this point need to use OAuth-based authentication."

The extension supported viewing multiple calendars across different Google accounts through either calendar sharing or separate Chrome profiles.

1	// The two unsupported-host affordances the popup controller (popup.js) renders
2	// for a host with no per-site source:
3	//
4	//   makeSourceRequestLink — shown when the generic extractor found a complete
5	//     event on an unlisted host (State 5): a small right-aligned "Suggest
6	//     Correction" link on the heading line that opens a prefilled GitHub "Event
7	//     source request" issue, seeded with the scraped event.
8	//   makePolicyLink — shown when there's nothing to show on a non-denylisted host
9	//     (State 3): a quiet "Disagree?" link beneath the empty-state glyph. Clicking
10	//     it does NOT navigate away — it EXPANDS the "how this extension finds events"
11	//     explanation inline into the popup body (buildPolicyPanel), so the user reads
12	//     it without losing their page, and continues via an "open an issue" link.
13	//
14	// An ES module, loaded on demand by popup.js via dynamic import(). The two
15	// `make*` functions are the controller's entry points; `buildSourceRequestUrl`
16	// and `buildIssueUrl` are also exported for the unit tests. The repo slug and
17	// template filename are exported too, so the unit tests assert against the single
18	// source of these strings (importing them) rather than re-hardcoding the literals.
19	// This is the source-request half of the former background.js.
20	//
21	// The "Suggest Correction" link targets the "Event source request" issue form
22	// (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/extractor-request.yml): a logged-in GitHub user lands
23	// on that structured form with the fields already filled in, reviews them, and
24	// clicks "Submit new issue" — no token, form service, or backend involved.
25	// GitHub forbids framing its pages (X-Frame-Options), so this opens in a new tab
26	// rather than being embedded, matching how the extension opens the Calendar
27	// template.
28	//
29	// The form applies the `extractor-request` label, which kicks off the
30	// auto-implement-extractor workflow — so a submitted request flows straight into
31	// the agent that writes the extractor and opens a PR.

## Reported-demand signal (repo-native, checked 2026-08-09)

The first *observable* answer to "which misses actually get reported" — and it is
mostly a negative one. As of 2026-08-09 the repo carries **13 issues labelled
[`extractor-request`](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues?q=label%3Aextractor-request)**,
and **every one was filed by the repo owner** (`missingbulb`). No external
reporter appears anywhere in that set. So the personas and pain points below
still rest on zero outside feedback; what follows is signal about the *channel*
and about one person's browsing, not about a user base.

- **The channel exists, is in-product, and fires at the failure moment — but it
  is gated behind a GitHub account.** The popup's unsupported-host states carry
  two affordances (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`): a "Suggest
  Correction" link when the generic extractor found a complete event on an
  unlisted host, and a "Disagree?" link that expands an inline "how this
  extension finds events" explanation ending in "open an issue". Both land the
  user on the repo's prefilled `extractor-request` issue form in a new tab —
  "no token, form service, or backend involved". Note the design *changed* from
  what was originally asked for: issue
  [#96](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/96)
  specified an **embedded Google Form** in the empty state, and the shipped
  implementation is a GitHub issue form instead, because GitHub forbids framing
  its pages (`X-Frame-Options`). The consequence for this wiki is the point: a
  reporter must be a logged-in GitHub user. That is a plausible — and
  **unverified** — explanation for why the external-report count is zero, and it
  is a friction this product otherwise spends all its design budget removing.
- **Reported demand skews local and civic, not global-platform.** Of the twelve
  site-specific requests, **eight name Israeli hosts** (`tel-aviv.gov.il`,
  `comy.co.il`, `cinema.co.il`, `secrettelaviv.com`, `barby.co.il`,
  `eventim.co.il`, `thinkdrink.co.il`, and `ticketmaster.co.il` — the local
  edition of a global platform), against only two genuinely international ones
  (`axs.com`, `bandsintown.com`). With a single reporter this is one person's
  browsing rather than a market shape, but it is worth holding as a hypothesis:
  the pages a person actually wants on their calendar are the small civic and
  venue sites near them, which are also the sites least likely to be served by a
  general AI tool trained on the majors.
- **A reported miss can be unfixable for reasons the user never sees — and the
  blocker is page *capture*, not extraction.** The `axs.com` request
  ([#285](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/285))
  was abandoned: AXS returns HTTP 403 to CI runners and the sandbox, so no real
  page HTML could be recorded, the pipeline refuses to invent `expected` values
  for a test case, and the owner closed it with *"Can't get the html to write an
  extractor for."* The `bandsintown.com` request
  ([#170](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/170))
  hit the identical 403 wall — the extractor was written but left uncompleted
  until a real browser supplied the page, after which it landed
  ([PR #199](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/pull/199)).
  So the sites most aggressive about bot-blocking are the ones least likely to
  gain a dedicated extractor, and from the user's side this looks like an
  arbitrary, permanent "no events found".

input.body:
Scheduled `product-wiki/wiki-growth` pass for slot `w2026-08-09` (dispatching issue #862). Web mode (WebSearch/WebFetch available), plus repo-native signal where the web had nothing to say.

**Never merge this automatically** — researched claims entering the wiki go through the review gate.

## Questions researched

**1. Users — "Which extraction misses actually get reported vs. silently tolerated?"** (open since the 2026-07-15 seed)

Answered, and answered *negatively*, from the repo's own record: all **13 `extractor-request` issues were filed by the repo owner**. This wiki still has zero outside-user signal, which is worth stating plainly rather than leaving the question open for a fourth pass. Three findings came out of looking:

- The report channel **exists, is in-product, and fires at the failure moment** — but it is gated behind a GitHub account. Issue #96 asked for an *embedded Google Form* in the "No events found" empty state; what shipped (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`) is a prefilled **GitHub issue form** opened in a new tab, because GitHub forbids framing its pages. A plausible (unverified) explanation for the zero.
- **Reported demand skews local/civic**: eight of the twelve site requests name Israeli hosts, only two a genuinely global platform. With one reporter this is a hypothesis, not a market shape — flagged as such.
- **A reported miss can be blocked by page *capture*, not extraction.** `axs.com` (#285) was abandoned because AXS returns HTTP 403 to CI runners, so no page HTML could be recorded and the pipeline refuses to invent `expected` values — the owner closed it with "Can't get the html to write an extractor for." `bandsintown.com` (#170) hit the identical wall and only landed once a browser supplied the page (PR #199). This is a new, distinct user-side pain point.

**2. Competitors — "Why did the incumbent vacate, and does that predict our cost curve?"** (surfaced 2026-07-26)

Answered, and **it corrects a claim this page made on 2026-07-26**. The chimbori shutdown note attributes the load to change requests from various Google teams (after the Calendar team declined to adopt the extension first-party), and the project's own wiki shows it carried an **OAuth integration with the Google Calendar Data API**, forced when Google killed API v2 in November 2014. Neither source blames the `hCalendar` page reader.

So the earlier clause — that the incumbent died of "the exact cost a rule-based per-site extractor set also accrues" — was an inference, not a finding. It is **struck in place with a note explaining why, not deleted**, and replaced with the sourced version: the cost that killed it attaches to the OAuth/API-integration surface this project deliberately does not have.

## Staleness spot-check

Re-fetched `github.com/chimbori/google-calendar-crx` (still live, notice unchanged) and its wiki. The Chrome Web Store / chrome-stats 403 wall recorded on 2026-07-26 was **not** re-attempted — the page's own open question says re-trying those hosts just burns budget.

| Page | Change |
|---|---|
| `product-wiki/Users/README.md` | New **Reported-demand signal** section; two new pain points; one open question retired, two opened; growth log; **Key insights** header added |
| `product-wiki/Competitors/README.md` | Superseded clause struck with a note + new sourced "died of platform integration" takeaway; one open question retired, one opened; growth log; **Key insights** header added |
| `product-wiki/Domain/README.md` | **Key insights** header only (see note below) |
| `product-wiki/Market/README.md` | **Key insights** header only (see note below) |

Nothing outside `product-wiki/` is touched, and `product-wiki/product-requirements/` is untouched.

**Note on Domain and Market**: all four wiki pages were missing the `## Key insights` header, which the product-wiki standard requires via two **blocking** checks (`product-wiki-page-sections`, `product-wiki-key-insights`) — a canon requirement the pages predate. Added to all four for conformance. Every bullet on Domain and Market distils a claim **already cited in that page's body**; no claim was added, changed or removed there, and no research was done on those two pages.

- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/96
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/285
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/170
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/pull/199

Competitors:
- https://github.com/chimbori/google-calendar-crx/wiki/Accounts-and-Authorization (the OAuth / Calendar Data API v2 statements)
- (the existing `chimbori/google-calendar-crx` README citation now carries the verbatim shutdown reasoning)

## Open questions left for the next run

- **Users** — Is the GitHub-account gate what keeps outside reports at zero, or is it just a small install base? The two are indistinguishable from inside the repo while install counts stay unobtainable.
- **Users** — Is the local/civic skew a property of demand or of the single reporter?
- **Competitors** — What *is* this project's own extractor maintenance cost curve? The incumbent precedent turned out not to answer it. Answerable from repo-native signal (extractor-fix commits, re-record runs) rather than the web — a good candidate for a repo-derived-mode run.
- **Competitors** — Chrome Web Store install counts still need a data route that isn't the two 403'd hosts.
- **Domain** — Do target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all; the per-host JSON-LD/fallback split; `.ics`-only event pages. All unchanged, all pointing at the fallback-coverage corpus.

{"number":869,"title":"product-wiki growth w2026-08-09: reported-demand signal, and what actually killed the incumbent","body":"Scheduled `product-wiki/wiki-growth` pass for slot `w2026-08-09` (dispatching issue #862). Web mode (WebSearch/WebFetch available), plus repo-native signal where the web had nothing to say.

**Never merge this automatically** — researched claims entering the wiki go through the review gate.

## Questions researched

**1. Users — "Which extraction misses actually get reported vs. silently tolerated?"** (open since the 2026-07-15 seed)

Answered, and answered *negatively*, from the repo's own record: all **13 `extractor-request` issues were filed by the repo owner**. This wiki still has zero outside-user signal, which is worth stating plainly rather than leaving the question open for a fourth pass. Three findings came out of looking:

- The report channel **exists, is in-product, and fires at the failure moment** — but it is gated behind a GitHub account. Issue #96 asked for an *embedded Google Form* in the "No events found" empty state; what shipped (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`) is a prefilled **GitHub issue form** opened in a new tab, because GitHub forbids framing its pages. A plausible (unverified) explanation for the zero.
- **Reported demand skews local/civic**: eight of the twelve site requests name Israeli hosts, only two a genuinely global platform. With one reporter this is a hypothesis, not a market shape — flagged as such.
- **A reported miss can be blocked by page *capture*, not extraction.** `axs.com` (#285) was abandoned because AXS returns HTTP 403 to CI runners, so no page HTML could be recorded and the pipeline refuses to invent `expected` values — the owner closed it with "Can't get the html to write an extractor for." `bandsintown.com` (#170) hit the identical wall and only landed once a browser supplied the page (PR #199). This is a new, distinct user-side pain point.

**2. Competitors — "Why did the incumbent vacate, and does that predict our cost curve?"** (surfaced 2026-07-26)

Answered, and **it corrects a claim this page made on 2026-07-26**. The chimbori shutdown note attributes the load to change requests from various Google teams (after the Calendar team declined to adopt the extension first-party), and the project's own wiki shows it carried an **OAuth integration with the Google Calendar Data API**, forced when Google killed API v2 in November 2014. Neither source blames the `hCalendar` page reader.

So the earlier clause — that the incumbent died of "the exact cost a rule-based per-site extractor set also accrues" — was an inference, not a finding. It is **struck in place with a note explaining why, not deleted**, and replaced with the sourced version: the cost that killed it attaches to the OAuth/API-integration surface this project deliberately does not have.

## Staleness spot-check

Re-fetched `github.com/chimbori/google-calendar-crx` (still live, notice unchanged) and its wiki. The Chrome Web Store / chrome-stats 403 wall recorded on 2026-07-26 was **not** re-attempted — the page's own open question says re-trying those hosts just burns budget.

## What changed, where

| Page | Change |
|---|---|
| `product-wiki/Users/README.md` | New **Reported-demand signal** section; two new pain points; one open question retired, two opened; growth log; **Key insights** header added |
| `product-wiki/Competitors/README.md` | Superseded clause struck with a note + new sourced "died of platform integration" takeaway; one open question retired, one opened; growth log; **Key insights** header added |
| `product-wiki/Domain/README.md` | **Key insights** header only (see note below) |
| `product-wiki/Market/README.md` | **Key insights** header only (see note below) |

Nothing outside `product-wiki/` is touched, and `product-wiki/product-requirements/` is untouched.

**Note on Domain and Market**: all four wiki pages were missing the `## Key insights` header, which the product-wiki standard requires via two **blocking** checks (`product-wiki-page-sections`, `product-wiki-key-insights`) — a canon requirement the pages predate. Added to all four for conformance. Every bullet on Domain and Market distils a claim **already cited in that page's body**; no claim was added, changed or removed there, and no research was done on those two pages.

## Citations added

Users:
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues?q=label%3Aextractor-request
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/96
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/285
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/170
- https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/pull/199

Competitors:
- https://github.com/chimbori/google-calendar-crx/wiki/Accounts-and-Authorization (the OAuth / Calendar Data API v2 statements)
- (the existing `chimbori/google-calendar-crx` README citation now carries the verbatim shutdown reasoning)

## Open questions left for the next run

- **Users** — Is the GitHub-account gate what keeps outside reports at zero, or is it just a small install base? The two are indistinguishable from inside the repo while install counts stay unobtainable.
- **Users** — Is the local/civic skew a property of demand or of the single reporter?
- **Competitors** — What *is* this project's own extractor maintenance cost curve? The incumbent precedent turned out not to answer it. Answerable from repo-native signal (extractor-fix commits, re-record runs) rather than the web — a good candidate for a repo-derived-mode run.
- **Competitors** — Chrome Web Store install counts still need a data route that isn't the two 403'd hosts.
- **Domain** — Do target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all; the per-host JSON-LD/fallback split; `.ics`-only event pages. All unchanged, all pointing at the fallback-coverage corpus.
